danish.title: Trettende bog (1812) — Kapitel 5
paragraphs: Næste dag stod den affældige Kutuzov tidligt op, som han havde bedt om, bad sine bønner, klædte sig på og steg med en ubehagelig bevidsthed om at skulle lede et slag, han ikke billigede, ind i sin karet og kørte fra Letasjovka (en landsby fem og en halv kilometer fra Tarutino) til det sted, hvor angrebskolonnerne skulle mødes. Han sad i kareten, døsede og vågnede skiftevis og lyttede efter enhver lyd af skydning fra højre som tegn på, at kampen var begyndt. Men alt var stille. En fugtig, grå efterårsmorgen var netop ved at bryde frem. Da Kutuzov nærmede sig Tarutino, lagde han mærke til kavalerister, der trak deres heste til vand på tværs af vejen, ad hvilken han kørte. Kutuzov betragtede dem indgående, standsede sin vogn og spurgte, hvilket regiment de tilhørte. De tilhørte en kolonne, der for længst burde have været langt foran i et baghold. »Det er måske en fejltagelse,« tænkte den gamle øverstkommanderende. Men lidt længere fremme så han infanteriregimenter med våbnene i pyramider og soldaterne, kun halvt påklædte, der spiste ruggrød og bar brænde. Han lod en officer hente. Officeren rapporterede, at der ikke var modtaget nogen ordre om at rykke frem.

»Hvad! Ikke mod...« begyndte Kutuzov, men standsede sig straks og sendte bud efter en højere officer. Da han var steget ud af sin karet, ventede han med sænket hoved, trak vejret tungt og gik tavst frem og tilbage. Da Ejkhen, den officer fra generalstaben, han havde tilkaldt, dukkede op, blev Kutuzov purpurrød i ansigtet, ikke fordi den officer var skyld i fejlen, men fordi han var et tilstrækkeligt vigtigt objekt at lade sin vrede gå ud over. Skælvende og stønnende faldt den gamle mand i det raseri, hvori han stundom plejede at vælte sig på jorden, og han fór løs på Ejkhen, truede ham med hænderne, råbte og overdængede ham med grove skældsord. En anden mand, kaptajn Brozin, der tilfældigvis dukkede op og slet ikke var til skyldig, led samme skæbne.
»Hvad er du for en anden slyngel? Jeg lader dig skyde! Skurke!« brølede Kutuzov med hæs stemme, viftede med armene og vaklede.

Han led fysisk. Han, øverstkommanderende, en Durchlauchtighed, om hvem alle sagde, at han sad inde med en magt, som ingen mand i Rusland nogensinde havde haft, at blive sat i denne situation — gjort til hele hærens nar! »Jeg behøvede ikke at have skyndt mig sådan med at bede i dag eller have ligget vågen hele natten og tænkt alting igennem,« tænkte han ved sig selv. »Da jeg var en grønskolling af en officer, ville ingen have vovet at gøre nar af mig sådan... og nu!« Han var i en tilstand af fysisk lidelse, som var det korporlig straf, og kunne ikke lade være med at give udtryk for den med råb af vrede og fortvivlelse. Men hans kræfter begyndte snart at svigte ham, og idet han så sig om med en bevidsthed om at have sagt meget, der ikke var på sin plads, steg han igen ind i sin karet og kørte tavst tilbage.

Hans vrede, en gang udløst, vendte ikke tilbage, og han lyttede blinkende svagt til undskyldninger og selvretfærdiggørelser (Jermolov kom først til ham næste dag) og til Bennigsens, Konovnitsyns og Tolls insisteren på, at den mislykket bevægelse burde udføres næste dag. Og endnu en gang måtte Kutuzov give sit samtykke.

english.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: The next day, the aging Kutuzov got up early, said his prayers, dressed, and with the unpleasant awareness of having to direct a battle he didn't approve of, climbed into his carriage and drove from Letashovka—a village three and a half miles from Tarutino—to where the attacking columns were supposed to assemble. He sat in the carriage, dozing and waking by turns, listening for any sound of gunfire on the right that would signal the action had begun. But everything was still quiet. A damp, gray autumn morning was just dawning. Approaching Tarutino, Kutuzov noticed cavalrymen leading their horses to water across the road he was driving along. He studied them closely, stopped his carriage, and asked what regiment they belonged to. They were part of a column that should have been far ahead, already in ambush position long before. 'Maybe it's a mistake,' thought the old commander in chief. But a little farther on, he saw infantry regiments with their weapons stacked, soldiers half-dressed, eating porridge and gathering firewood. He sent for an officer. The officer reported that no order to advance had been received.

'What! Not rec—' Kutuzov began, but caught himself and sent for a senior officer. Getting out of his carriage, he stood with his head drooping, breathing heavily, pacing silently up and down. When Eykhen, the staff officer he'd summoned, appeared, Kutuzov turned purple in the face—not because Eykhen was to blame, but because he was a sufficiently important target for his fury. Trembling and gasping, the old man fell into one of those rages in which he sometimes used to roll on the ground. He fell on Eykhen, shaking his fists, shouting and heaping vile abuse on him. Another officer, Captain Brozin, who happened to appear and was not at all to blame, suffered the same fate.
'What kind of scoundrel are you? I'll have you shot! Blackguards!' Kutuzov yelled in a hoarse voice, waving his arms and staggering.

He was suffering physically. He—the commander in chief, a Serene Highness whom everyone said held powers no man in Russia had ever possessed—to be put in this position, made the laughingstock of the whole army! 'I needn't have rushed to pray this morning, or stayed up all night thinking everything through,' he thought. 'When I was a young officer, no one would have dared mock me like this... and now!' He was in a state of physical anguish, as if he'd been beaten, and couldn't help expressing it through cries of anger and distress. But his strength soon gave out. Looking around, conscious of having said too much, he climbed back into his carriage and drove away in silence.

His rage, once spent, didn't return. Blinking wearily, he listened to excuses and justifications (Ermolov didn't come to see him until the next day) and to the insistence of Bennigsen, Konovnitsyn, and Toll that the failed operation should be attempted again the following day. Once more, Kutuzov had to consent.
